title: The Other Phone
hook: A user changes their account password after losing an old phone. Hours later the old phone is still logged in and can still like, comment and send messages. Your job is to log that session out.
context: Social app with mobile clients, access tokens, and a backend serving 1,000 requests per second.
solution_brief: Revocation needs server-side state. Enforce on the server, revoke every other session after a security event, keep the check on a fast store, and bound the stale-trust window with invalidation events and short TTLs. Stateless tokens need a session id or token version to be revocable. Server decides, the device is irrelevant. Password change revokes all sessions except the current one. In-memory validity check on every request. Revocation events plus short TTLs bound the window.

steps.prompt: Your app issues a signed token valid for 30 days, and the server checks only the signature and expiry. After a password change, what lets the server reject a token it issued earlier?
steps.context_note: Pure stateless tokens cannot be taken back.

options.text: Nothing needs changing, because the signature check already rejects tokens from before the change
A server-side session ID or per-user token version that tokens must match
A push notification asking the old phone to delete its token

steps.explanation: A purely stateless token carries no way to be taken back, so the server needs state to compare against, such as a session record or a per-user token version. The signature stays valid after a password change, and rotating the signing key logs out every user instead of this one.
steps.bottleneck_note: Revocation requires state. Stateless tokens trade revocability for scale.

steps.prompt: What makes the token on that phone useless?
steps.context_note: The old phone is offline and may never contact your server again, so you cannot tell it to log out.

options.text: Remotely wiping the phone as soon as it next comes online
Pushing a logout message the next time the phone connects to the app
Shortening the token lifetime for future logins
Invalidating the session on the server side so the token is refused

steps.explanation: A token is only useful when it is presented to your server, and the server decides whether to honour it. Once the session is invalid, the copy on the device is worthless even if the device never hears about it. Remote wipe and push messages depend on reaching the phone, and a shorter lifetime for future logins does not touch the existing token.
steps.bottleneck_note: Enforce on the server, which you control, not on the device, which you do not.

steps.prompt: The user is signed in on three phones and changes their password on the one in their hand. Which sessions should the server end?
steps.context_note: The user suspects that someone else has their login.

options.text: All sessions except the one that just changed the password
Only the session that has gone the longest without any activity
None, so the user is not forced to sign in again

steps.explanation: A password change usually means the user suspects compromise, so every other session should end while the freshly authenticated one stays. Picking by idle time or age is arbitrary and leaves risky sessions alive, and doing nothing leaves the suspected intruder logged in.
steps.bottleneck_note: Security events should invalidate everything except the proven-fresh session.

steps.prompt: Where should the per-request validity check read from, so that latency stays low?
steps.context_note: Every request must now be checked against session state, on a service that served 1,000 requests per second with no lookups.

options.text: Each API server's local memory, loaded once when the server starts
Nowhere on routine requests: check only at login, when the token is issued
A fast shared store keyed by session ID, backed by the database

steps.explanation: A fast store in front of the database keeps the check cheap while the database stays authoritative, and the cache lifetime sets the revocation window. Local memory loaded at startup never sees later revocations, and checking only at login is the same as having no revocation.
steps.bottleneck_note: Put the validity check on a fast store so the hot path stays hot.

steps.prompt: Which change most reduces how long the old phone can keep posting after the session is deleted?
steps.context_note: Session deletion runs as an asynchronous job, and API nodes cache each validity check.

options.text: Lengthen the cache lifetime so that fewer checks reach the session store
Push revocation events that clear node caches, with short TTLs
Make the deletion job run faster and leave the caches as they are
Ask the app to clear its token at its next launch

steps.explanation: The stale window is the job's delay plus the cache lifetime, so clearing caches on a revocation event and keeping TTLs short attacks both parts, and sensitive actions can skip the cache for an authoritative check. A faster deletion job leaves stale cache entries, and relying on the old phone to cooperate gives the attacker the choice.
steps.bottleneck_note: Know your staleness bound, and tighten it where the risk is highest.
